captions.label: 2a
captions.caption: Fig. 2a displays that 45.50 % of Cr(VI) removal was observed within 12 h in the Bio-FeS system, the reason for this is that Cr(VI) could be adsorbed onto the surface of Bio-FeS. Obviously, Cr(VI) removal effi­ ciencies remain unchanged later, which suggests Cr(VI) adsorption had reached equilibrium after 12 h. Additionally, the Cr(VI) removal process was fitted well with the first-order kinetic model. The first-order rate constant (k) for the Cr(VI) removal by MR-1/Bio-FeS (0.099 h−1) were significantly higher than that by MR-1 alone (0.008 h−1), this was because Bio-FeS could act as an excellent electron shuttle to accelerate the EET rate from MR-1 to Cr(VI), thus significantly accelerating the Cr (VI) reduction. Fig. 2b displays that with the rapid removal of Cr(VI) from the solution, the Cr(total) concentration in the solution also sharply decreased in the MR-1/Bio-FeS system, and the Cr(total) removal effi­ ciency reached 99.1 % within 48 h. However, the Cr(III) concentration in the solution was relatively low during the whole process, e.g. the Cr (III) concentration was only 0.26 mg/L within 48 h. These results in­ dicates that the MR-1/Bio-FeS system can efficiently remove Cr(VI) and Cr(total) from solution simultaneously.

captions.label: 3b
captions.caption: Fig. 3b displays that the Cr(VI) removal efficiency by MR-1/Bio-FeS was significantly increased with an increase in cell concentration. Approximately 81.18 % of Cr(VI) removal was reached with the cell concentration of OD600 of 0.3. While Cr(VI) can be completely removed within 48, 36 and 24 h with the cell concentration of OD600 of 0.4, 0.5 and 0.6, respectively. This result was supported by our previous study reported that the Cr(VI) removal efficiency by nZVI/MR-1 increased with cell concentrations [27,28].

captions.label: 3c
captions.caption: Fig. 3c displays Cr(VI) removal was highly pH-dependent, the Cr(VI) removal efficiencies were 95.3 %, 81.5 %, 82.2 %, and 73.9 % after 48 h for the MR-1/Bio-FeS systems with the initial pH of 5, 6.5, 9, and 12, respectively. The maximum Cr(VI) removal was observed under weakly acidic conditions, this may be due to the increase in enzymatic activity of MR-1 under weakly acidic conditions, which was consistent with the previous finding [27]. Similar conclusions have been observed by Zhang et al. (2022), suggesting that the optimum pH for Cr(VI) removal by Shewanella putrefaciens coupled with riboflavin was about 6.0 [13]. captions.caption: Fig. 1 | Biosynthesis pathway of enterobactin in Escherichia coli. The biosynthesis of enterobactin involves the synthesis of 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate from chorismate by three enzymes: EntA, EntB and EntC. Enterobactin is then formed by assembling three molecules of DHB and three l-serines, facilitated by the non-ribosomal peptide synthetases EntF together with EntE and EntD

Fig. 2 | Biosynthesis pathway of pyoverdine I in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. a, The precursor of the siderophore pyoverdine I is an 11-amino acid peptide that is assembled in the cytoplasm of Pseudomonas aeruginosa cells by four non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs), namely, PvdL, PvdI, PvdJ and PvdD. Additionally, three enzymes (PvdH, PvdA and PvdF) are involved in synthesizing atypical amino acids utilized by the NRPS. PvdL is the NRPS involved in the assembling of the tripeptide l-Glu–d-Tyr–l-Dab (in blue like PvdL). Next, d-Ser, l-Arg, d-Ser and l-fOHOrn (all in green) are incorporated successively by PvdI, l-Lys and l-fOHOrn (in pink) by PvdJ, and the two l-Thr (in yellow) by PvdD. From the initial step of peptide assembly, a myristate or myristoleate chain is incorporated on the first residue (l-Glu) by PvdL. b, The cytoplasmic precursor is exported to the periplasm, where it undergoes maturation involving other enzymes

Fig. 3 | Structures of siderophores. Shown are structures of different siderophores. Highlighted in blue are the catechol chelating groups; in green the hydroxamates; in pink the carboxylates and in orange the phenolates. The stereochemistry of the chemical structures of the siderophores presented is not specified.

Fig. 4 | Iron uptake in Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. a, Siderophore–Fe transport through the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. Iron uptake begins with the translocation of siderophore–Fe complexes across the outer membrane by TonB-dependent transporters (TBDTs)15. Each siderophore or closely related siderophore has a specific TBDT that facilitates its uptake by the bacterial cells. The energy required for this transport is provided by the TonB–ExbB–ExbD complex. This complex functions as a molecular ‘motor’, which transmits energy from the inner membrane proton motive force to the TBDT in the outer membrane, facilitating the translocation of the siderophore–iron complex into the periplasm94–96. More TBDTs are expressed than TonB–ExbB–ExbD complexes, indicating that a single TonB–ExbB–ExbD complex interacts with several TBDTs. b, Iron release from siderophores in Gram-negative bacteria. After the uptake of siderophore–Fe complexes across the outer membrane, the release of iron from the siderophore can occur either in the periplasm or the cytoplasm, depending on the siderophore and bacterial species16. In the first case, after its dissociation from the chelator, iron associates with periplasmic binding proteins (PBPs) to avoid any precipitation and is then transported across the inner membrane by a specific ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter. In the second case, the siderophore–Fe binds in the periplasm to a PBP associated with an ABC transporter, which transports the siderophore–Fe complex further across the inner membrane. Iron release from siderophores always involves an iron reduction step, which can be associated or not with a chemical modification or hydrolysis of the siderophore.

Fig. 5 | Iron acquisition by enterobactin and pyoverdine I. a, Iron acquisition by enterobactin in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Escherichia coli. Iron acquisition by enterobactin (Ent) in P. aeruginosa and E. coli is a process characterized by distinct mechanisms in each bacterium. P. aeruginosa does not produce the enterobactin siderophore but can utilize it. Upon the formation of the Ent–Fe complex in the environment of P. aeruginosa, recognition is facilitated by the TonB-dependent transporters (TBDTs) PfeA and PirA, with PfeA acting as the primary TBDT for this siderophore–Fe complex and PirA as the secondary TBDT199–201. Following transport across the outer membrane by TBDTs, the iron complex dissociates from Ent in the periplasm. This step involves iron reduction and hydrolysis of Ent into three molecules of 2,3-dihydroxybenzoic acid (DHBS) catalysed by the esterase PfeE103. By contrast, in E. coli, a single TBDT, FepA, is involved in the import of the Ent–Fe complex across the outer membrane202–204. Within the periplasm, the Ent–Fe complex binds to the periplasmic protein FepB, which is associated with an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter, FepBC, facilitating import across the inner membrane205–207. The dissociation of iron from Ent in the cytoplasm involves a reductase, Ydjh, and an esterase, Fes, similar to the process observed in the periplasm of P. aeruginosa, resulting in the hydrolysis of Ent into three DHBS molecules104. b, Iron acquisition by pyoverdine I in P. aeruginosa. Pyoverdine I (Pvd) is the primary siderophore synthesized and excreted by P. aeruginosa. When Pvd has chelated iron in the bacterial environment, the complex is recognized and transported across the outer membrane by two TBDTs, namely, FpvA and FpvB208–210. FpvA is the major transporter, whereas FpvB functions as the secondary transporter211,212. Within the periplasm, the Pvd–Fe complex associates with two periplasmic proteins, FpvF and FpvC108. FpvF belongs to the periplasmic siderophore-binding protein, and FpvC to the periplasmic iron-binding proteins108,213. The FpvF–Pvd–Fe–FpvC complex further associates with the inner membrane complex FpvGHJK, where FpvG functions as a reductase, and the functions of the other three proteins (FpvH, FpvJ and FpvK) remain unknown but are essential for optimal reductase activity of FpvG106,107,214. Iron is reduced within the FpvCFGHJK complex and dissociated from Pvd106,107. The ferrous iron is then specifically chelated by FpvC213, which transports it to the ABC transporter FpvDE for translocation into the cytoplasm108. Pvd remains associated with FpvF, which guides it to the PvdRT–OpmQ efflux pump, facilitating its export into the extracellular milieu214–216. As Pvd undergoes no chemical modification or degradation during the iron release process, it can readily chelate another ferric ion, initiating the cycle anew105.

captions.caption: Fig. 1 evaluates the impact of AGS formation on the pollutants removal. Overall, the AGSBR system achieved efficient removal of conventional pollutants (COD, TN, and TP) and TC, with a progressive increase in pollutant removal observed as sludge granulation advanced. Initially, flocculent activated sludge (Phase I) exhibited relatively low removal efficiencies for COD (55.2%), TN (56.1%), and TP (52.3%) (Fig. 1a), the possible reason could be due to the microbial inhibition of TC. However, during the initial phase of AGS formation (Phase II), the removal rates of COD, TN, and TP significantly improved, reaching 78.85%, 77.86%, and 56.18%, respectively, indicating that sludge granulation markedly enhanced effluent quality. Upon reaching the maturation phase (Phase III), the removal rates further increased to 87.4% for COD, 84.1% for TN, and 66.5% for TP. Notably, TP removal exhibited a less pronounced increase compared to COD and TN, poten­ tially due to the inhibitory effects of TC on polyphosphate-accumulating organisms (PAOs), as previously revealed by Nivedhita et al (Nivedhita et al., 2022). As shown in Fig. 1b, TC removal also improved substan­ tially, increasing from 63.0% during Phase I to 82.4% in Phase II, and stabilizing above 83% in the mature AGS phase (Phase III). These findings demonstrate the robust performance and adaptability of the AGS system in treating TC-containing wastewater. The primary mech­ anisms responsible for TC removal include surface adsorption by gran­ ules and microbial biodegradation (Wang et al., 2021). Additionally, the abundant secretion of EPS with adsorption capabilities during AGS formation process plays a crucial role in TC removal (Peng et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2022).

Fig. 2 shows the 80-h Cr(VI) reduction performance by S. oneidensis MR-1 in MSM. In the presence of CQDs, the Cr(VI) concentration decreased by 0.06 mM after 80 h, which closely matched the concen­ tration in the control check (CK) sample with Cr(VI) alone, suggesting that CQDs did not directly remove Cr(VI). The Cr(VI) reduction effi­ ciency by S. oneidensis MR-1 alone was <50 % (Fig. 2A). Notably, as the concentration of CQDs gradually elevated from 14 to 70 mg/L, the Cr (VI) reduction efficiency increased from 68.1 % to 99.6 %. Importantly, the pseudo-first-order kinetic model did not adequately describe Cr(VI) reduction in the absence of CQDs (Fig. S3), whereas the pseudo-second- order model exhibited a superior fit. This suggests that factors beyond the concentration of Cr(VI), such as the number of degrading active cells, may also limit the reduction rate. This finding contrasted sharply with our previous report, in which the reduction of nitrobenzene by S. oneidensis MR-1 followed first-order kinetics (Wang et al., 2020). Some researchers attributed similar phenomena to Cr(VI) toxicity and the accumulation of reduction products, which may decrease the pop­ ulation of reactive S. oneidensis MR-1 cells (Yu et al., 2024). Neverthe­ less, the coefficient of determination (R²) of the pseudo-first-order model for Cr(VI) reduction increased with higher CQD concentrations (Fig. S3), indicating that the S. oneidensis MR-1 cells were activated by the CQDs.

captions.caption: Figure 1. Schematic representation of the possible steps in the metabolism of aerobic methanotrophic bacteria. O2 is used in the oxidation of CH4 to methanol in the first step catalyzed by MMO enzymes (represented by the pMMO in this scheme). This first step may also be performed in the cytoplasm by the sMMO in methanotrophic bacteria possessing this enzyme. Methanol is converted to formaldehyde by methanol dehydrogenase (MDH); formaldehyde can be assimilated into cellular compounds (via the ribulose monophosphate (RuMP) cycle in gammaproteobacterial MOB or via the serine cycle in alphaproteobacterial MOB) or be oxidized to formate by formaldehyde dehydrogenases (FADH); formate is then oxidized to CO2 by formate dehydrogenases (FDH). O2 is the terminal electron acceptor in aerobic respiration, while other oxidants can potentially serve as terminal electron acceptors in methanotrophic bacteria performing anaerobic respiration under O2-limiting conditions. Under O2 limitation, carbon that enters the RuMP cycle can go through fermentation for energy generation as opposed to respiration. ∗Iron (Fe3+) and manganese (Mn4+) reduction would presumably occur outside the cell, via extracellular electron transfer, and could potentially be mediated by electron shuttles or microbial consortia. This figure was created with BioRender.

Figure 2. Schematic representation of methane (CH4) oxidation zones in seasonally or permanently stratified lakes with anoxic hypolimnia and sediments. Shown are typical profiles of dissolved oxygen (O2), CH4, and carbon stable isotope composition of CH4 and the methanotrophic microorganisms commonly found in each layer. In the oxic and hypoxic portions of the water column, alphaproteobacterial and gammaproteobacterial MOB can be found, with gammaproteobacterial MOB often more abundant in hypoxic waters, as indicated by bold fonts. Gammaproteobacterial MOB, “Ca. Methylomirabilota”, and anaerobic methanotrophic archaea (ANME) can be present in anoxic hypolimnia and sediments.The abundance, activity, and importance of each methanotrophic group to the total CH4 consumption in each of the layers may vary with the ecosystem. Methanotrophic bacteria in the “Ca. Methylomirabilota” (formerly NC10) phylum aerobically oxidize CH4 under anoxic conditions through intracellular O2 production from nitrite.

Figure 3. Graphical depiction of hypotheses for the presence of MOB (ovals) in microoxic or anoxic waters of stratified lakes. The panels show the counter gradient of O2 (top) and CH4 (bottom) in water columns and the sediment (horizontal bar below). a. under anoxic conditions, MOB cells could be inactive, either dormant or dead; b. under microoxic conditions, MOB may aerobically oxidize CH4 and perform fermentation with the release of CH4-derived organic compounds and low biomass accumulation; c. downward O2 diffusive flux or episodic O2 intrusions due to water column instability could supply O2 to MOB to oxidize CH4 aerobically at depths that appear anoxic at the time of sampling; d. O2 supply via local photosynthetic O2 production could sustain aerobic CH4 oxidation by MOB in seemingly anoxic waters (filaments depict oxygenic photosynthetic microorganisms); e. MOB could potentially use alternative electron acceptors (AEA) to oxidize CH4 and/or perform anaerobic respiration under anoxic conditions, which could involve the participation of other microorganisms (squares) in syntrophic relationships with MOB.

Abbreviations: Ack, acetate kinase; CoB-HS, coenzyme B; CODH/ACS, CO dehydrogenase/acetyl-CoA synthase complex; CoM-SH, coenzyme M; F420, F420 coenzyme; Fd, ferredoxin; Fpo, F420H2:methanophenazine oxidoreductase; FrhB, Coenzyme F420 hydrogenase subunit beta; Ftr, formylmethanofuran-H4SPT formyltransferase; Fwd, formyl-methanofuran dehydrogenase; H4SPT, tetrahydrosarcinapterin; Hdr, heterodisulﬁde reductase; HSCoA, coenzyme A; Mch, methylene-H4SPT cyclohydrolase; Mcr, methyl-CoM reductase; Mer, F420-dependent methylene-H4SPT reductase; MFR, methanofuran; MP, methanophenazine; Mtd, F420-dependent methylene H4SPT dehydrogenase; Mtr, Na+-translocating methyl-H4SPT:coenzyme M (CoM) methyltransferase; Rnf, homolog of the Rhodobacter nitrogen ﬁxation complex. The reversible methanogenesis pathway (left) is adapted from Yan et al. and Ferry et al . [47,61].

Figure 4. Conceptual representation of biogeochemical cycles associated with electrochemically driven methane oxidation across geochemical zones. The special metabolism of methane-oxidizing bacteria (MOB) under microaerobic conditions enables coupling of methane oxidation to extracellular electron transfer (EET)-linked biogeochemical cycles, including direct Fe(III)/Mn(IV) reduction (1), or intermediate-dependent synergistic interactions with bacterial partners for more diverse elemental (Fe, Mn, Cr, and As) cycles (2). In anoxic zones, anaerobic methanotrophic archaea (ANME) use EET pathways to couple anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM) to direct Fe(III)/Mn(IV) reduction (3), reduction of humic substances and analogs like pyrogenic carbon (4), Cr(VI) (5), and As(V) (6), or through direct interspecies electron transfer with sulfate-reducing bacteria for sulfate reduction (7). Certain methanogens can also couple AOM to Fe(III) reduction via direct EET (8) or through intermediate-dependent synergistic interactions with metal-reducing bacteria (9). AOM-linked biogeochemical cycles can also interact with each other: humic substances and pyrogenic carbon can function as electron snorkels to facilitate Fe(III)- and Mn(IV)-dependent AOM (10); iron minerals can interact with and stimulate humic-dependent (11) and sulfate-dependent AOM (12); humic or iron minerals can mediate methane oxidation coupled to CO2 reduction (13) or N2O reduction (14).

Figure 5. Potential applications of electrochemically driven methane oxidation. (A) bioremediation, through the direct reductive remediation by anaerobic methanotrophic archaea (1), or synergistic pathway between methane-oxidizing bacteria and contaminant reducers (2), or methane-fueled cathodic contaminants reduction (3). (B) greenhouse gas mitigation to remove dissolved methane in the efﬂuent of anaerobic wastewater treatment (1), or inhibit on-site methane emissions via material amendment to enhance methane oxidation (2). (C) production of value-added chemicals via electrofermentation (1), or via methane-fueled selective cathodic reactions (2). (D) Electricity generation.

(B) Schematic of the interdigitated microelectrode array (IDA), consisting of two 10-­μm-­wide working electrodes separated by a 5-­μm gap. Biomass was dried onto the IDA to promote physical contact with the electrode surface. Conductance was determined from the linear slope of the current-­voltage relationship measured across the two working electrodes. (C) ANME-­1/Desulfofervidus, ANME-­2a/Seep-­SRB1, and ANME-­2a+2c/Seep-­ SRB1+2 consortia and G. sulfurreducens electrogenic biofilm show high conductance when dried on the indium tin oxide (ITO) IDAs, whereas G. sulfurreducens nonelec- trogenic planktonic cell pellets show low conductance. Black dashed lines indicate the means of the data points. Representative light microscopy of IDAs with dried biomass is shown above the sample names; see fig. S7 for enlarged microscopy images. Dashed line area in the blank indicates the working electrode area of an ITO IDA. The number of biological replicates is included in brackets after the sample names. (D) Dry conduction measurements of ANME-­1/Desulfofervidus consortia on different IDA materials show comparable conductances. Black dashed lines indicate the means of the data points. The number of biological replicates is included in brackets after the material types. (E) Dry conduction of ANME-­1/Desulfofervidus and ANME-­2a+2c/Seep-­SRB1+2 consortia remains the same with paraformaldehyde (PFA) fixation but decreases with heating and oxygen exposure. Solid lines represent linear regressions of the plotted data, and shaded areas represent the 95% confidence intervals of the linear regressions.

Fig. 2. Cyclic voltammetry measurements of dried and live ANME/SRB consortia. (A) Live biomass was pressed onto the IDA using a Gelrite plug in a syringe to pro- mote physical attachment and electrochemistry measurements under anoxic conditions in PBS solution (pH 7.4). A platinum wire served as the counter electrode and Ag/ AgCl (1 M KCl) as the reference electrode. (B) Representative cyclic voltammograms of dry-­deposited and live ANME-­1/Desulfofervidus consortia show clear redox signals, whereas PBS and Gelrite backgrounds show no redox signal. (C) Representative cyclic voltammograms show redox peaks in diverse ANME/SRB consortia after subtraction of PBS background current from the same IDAs. (D) Comparison of peak current heights for ANME-­1/Desulfofervidus consortia subjected to increasing scan rates, revealing a linear dependence on the square root of scan rates and indicating that electron transport through the consortia is rate limiting.

Fig. 3. Generator-­collector measurements of ANME/SRB consortia. (A and B) Schematics of expected outcomes for generator-­collector measurements: (A) a blank background lacking conductive material and (B) ANME/SRB consortia containing redox conductive cytochromes that mediate electron transport across the 5-­μm gap. The generator electrode sweeps to a more negative potential, reducing the redox component, while the collector electrode is held at a constant positive potential, reoxidizing it. (C and D) Current measured at the generator electrode sweeping from +335 to −265 mV for (C) backgrounds and (D) live ANME/SRB consortia. (E and F) Currents mea- sured at the collector electrodes holding at a constant +335 mV for (E) backgrounds and (F) live ANME/SRB consortia. Together, the generator-­collector measurements reveal that the redox-­active components, consistent with multiheme cytochrome c, in diverse ANME/SRB consortia are capable of facilitating micrometer-­scale electron transport from generator electrodes to collector electrodes.

Fig. 4. Redox properties of cytochromes in model electroactive organisms and syntrophic consortia. Electron transport routes and the reduction potentials of key components in (A) Geobacter, (B) Shewanella, (C) syntrophic consortia of SRB and methanogen based on interspecies hydrogen transfer, and (D) syntrophic consortia of ANME and SRB based on direct interspecies electron transport. Black lines indicate the midpoint reduction potentials. Gray bars indicate the reduction potential windows of multiheme cytochromes. The midpoint reduction potentials of cytochromes are more positive than their electron acceptors, but their broad redox-­active windows al- low reactions to occur. (E) Compilation of reduction potential windows show window size increase with increasing number of hemes in purified cytochromes. The large multiheme cytochrome c (MHC) in ANME/SRB consortia could have even broader redox-­active windows to facilitate electron transport to electron acceptors at a large range of reduction potentials.

captions.caption: Fig. 1. Redox balancing strategies used by PNSB during anaerobic photoheterotrophic growth on a reduced carbon source. captions.caption: Fig. 1. R. palustris as a biotechnology chassis. R. palustris is a metabolically diverse purple non-sulfur bacterium and a developing biotechnology chassis. R. palustris has been applied in many applications such as developing a deeper fundamental understanding of tradeoffs between metabolisms, biodegradation, biofuels, bio­ plastics, electricity systems, and agricultural production.

Fig. 2. The major metabolic core states that R. palustris is renowned for flexibly switching between. Under anaerobic conditions, R. palustris generates ATP through cyclic phos­ phorylation from light whereby electrons are cycled through a proton-pumping electron transport chain rather than using a terminal electron acceptor. It can use either organic com­ pounds (photoheterotrophic) or inorganic compounds and CO2 (photoautotrophic). Note that there are tradeoffs in uti­ lizing reducing potential between biomass production, poly­ hydroxyalkanoate formation, and nitrogen fixation. Under aerobic conditions without light, R. palustris employs proton motive force to transfer electrons to a terminal electron acceptor (e.g. O2, dimethyl sulfoxide, potassium nitrate, or sodium nitrite) to produce a hydrogen gradient and ultimately generate ATP for energy. In this case, R. palustris uses either organic compounds (chemoheterotrophy) or inorganic elec­ trons donors and CO2 (chemoautotrophy) under aerobic conditions.
Fig. 3. Highlights of biohydrogen production by R. palustris from versatile feedstocks and novel strategies for enhancement.

Fig. 4. Electricity generation by R. palustris. Due to its flexible and robust metabolism, several types of bioelectrochemical systems involving R. palustris have been engineered, which can utilize renewable feedstocks for the generation of power and other applications.

Fig. 5. Bioplastic production by the metabolically versatile R. palustris. It can produce monomers and copolymers of polyhydroxyalkanoates from various renewable and sustainable feedstocks. Its ability to produce several co-product streams also make R. palustris an ideal candidate for engineering toward industrial production.

captions.caption: Figure 1 | Activity of the TAOM consortia in culture. a, The exponential increase of sulfide production translates to a doubling time of 68 days (biological replicates n 5 4). b, Representative fluorescence micrograph of TAOM consortia from a; red, ANME-1; green, HotSeep-1. Scale bar, 10 mm. Representative of 14 similar images recorded. c, Sulfide production under TAOM conditions (red circles, 0.07 mM sulfide per day) versus a control (white squares, 0.02mM per day). Hydrogen (blue triangles), or hydrogen plus methane (purple stars) increased sulfide production (both 0.55 mM per day; biological replicates n 5 3, symbols represent mean values, error bars are s.d.). d, Per cent of total RNA reads mapped to ANME-1 (red) and HotSeep-1 (green) after 3 days of incubation (c), biological replicates n 5 3, data are mean values, for statistical analyses see Supplementary Table 1.

Figure 2 | Hydrogen in TAOM cultures. a, Hydrogen gas pressure under TAOM conditions (methane, 0.2 MPa; sulfate, 28 mM; 5-day incubation (filled circle)). The dashed arrow depicts gas phase exchange with methane. Open circles show equilibration of hydrogen in the headspace (n 5 1). b, Hydrogen production in 10 ml TAOM culture supplied with 0.2 MPa methane after headspace exchange and addition of 10 mM molybdate (final concentration) to inhibit hydrogen consumption. Open circles are replicate measurements with hydrogen production of 2 and 3 nmol l21 min21. Dotted line is predicted hydrogen production for reverse methanogenesis (CH4 1 2H2O R CO2 1 4H2) 5 420nmol H2 l21 min21 culture, for an observed sulfide production rate of 104nmol l21 min21. Both experiments were repeated once with the same results.

Figure 3 | Expression of genes and visualization of structures attributed to interspecies electron transfer in TAOM. a, Expression of archaeal (red) and bacterial (green) genes in incubations with hydrogen (darker shade), or hydrogen plus methane (lighter shade), relative to methane alone (expression under TAOM condition 5 1;biological replicates n 5 3; *P , 0.05; for statistics see Supplementary Table 5b). b–f, Micrographs of thin sections. Scale bars, 300nm. b–d, TAOM consortia with HotSeep-1 cells (H; rod-shaped; approximately 13 0.5 mm) and ANME-1 cells (A; cylindrical shape with envelope30; 1.53 0.8 mm). Nanowires of 10 nm diameter and up to several thousand nanometres in length connect both species, representative of 70 recorded images. c, d, Arrows mark the apparent origin of the wires from the membrane of HotSeep-1 bacteria to the polar sites of ANME-1 cells. d, HotSeep-1 cell with nanowires crossing the cell membrane (marked by the arrow). e, f, Aggregated HotSeep-1 cells grown with hydrogen do not develop nanowires; representative of 48 images.

captions.caption: Fig. 2a displays the relative abundance of microorganisms at the phylum level. After the enrichment culture of MOB was completed, microbial sequencing was performed, and the results are shown in Fig. 2a. MOB represented the original soil sample in the C0 stage, which was just inoculated into the soil without the addition of zeolites. The initial inoculum for the enrichment of MOB was predominantly composed of Proteobacteria (81 %), which includes all known meth­ anotrophs and methylotrophs. However, the most abundant phylum in the Raw and K2 groups shifted to Gram-positive Firmicutes (both around 63 %) during C2. Further comparison at the order level within the Raw and K2 groups revealed distinct dominant bacterial categories. In C2- Raw, Alicyclobacillus and Bacillales were the predominant orders, ac­ counting for 38.24 % and 16.76 %, respectively (Fig. 2b). Conversely, the K2 group was primarily characterized by the electroactive bacteria Clostridia and Thermincolales, comprising 24.7 % and 17.3 %, respec­ tively (Fig. 2c). Over the long-term cultivation, the prevalence of Fir­ micutes decreased, and Proteobacteria emerged as the dominant group, constituting over 80 % of the microbial community in all four groups. At the genus level, methanotroph was dominated by Methylocystis (up 7.3 %) (Fig. S2). Additionally, a group within the Nitrospirota phylum, accounting for less than 0.1 % of the total community, was almost entirely composed of Nitrospira spp. Notably, this bacterial species be­ longs to the complete ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (Comammox) group, capable of achieving complete nitrification from NH4 + to NO3 - [24,25]. MOB produce a considerable amount of EPS [33], consisting mainly of extracellular polysaccharides (EPSs), extracellular proteins (ECPs), and nucleic acids. EPS can be categorized into S-EPS, LB-EPS, and TB-EPS. EPS serve not only as components of cellular defense but also as mediators for extracellular electron shuttling [37]. In this study, EPSs constituted the majority of the EPS components compared with ECPs. EPSs accounted for over 70 % of the total EPS in most groups. Among these fractions, S-EPS (average 1.38 ± 0.48 mg g−1 in C2) was higher than LB-EPS and TB-EPS by about 4-fold, which is attributable to increased soluble metabolic byproducts generated during the rapid growth of the microbial community. Notably, the K2 group exhibited a marked increase in all EPS components during the C2 stage, with the total amounts of S-EPSs and LB-EPSs reaching up to 1.86 ± 0.27 mg g−1

Fig. 2 shows the growth of methanotrophic biomass for the different N sources, O2 concentrations, and CH4-delivery pressures. To under­ stand the effects of nitrogen and O2 (stage I), we evaluated biomass growth for two static O2 levels (limited vs saturated O2) along with two nitrogen sources, NH4 + and NO3 −. In stage I, the methanotrophic biomass had a faster and more extensive growth with NH4 +-N as the N-source, compared with NO3 −-N (Fig. 2(a)). Several studies observed that methanotrophs grew faster with NH4 + than with NO3 −, since NH4 + already is at the −3 oxidation state needed for incorporation into amino acids and nucleic acids (Zhang et al., 2017; Bordel et al., 2019b; Rodríguez et al., 2020a). The biomass grown with the NH4 +-N reached ~0.6 and ~0.5 optical OD600 under static limited and saturated DO levels, respectively, but the biomass grown with NO3 −-N reached only ~0.2 for both O2 levels. More quan­ titatively, the NH4 +-N utilization rates for limited- and saturated-O2 conditions were 3.1 ± 0.1 mg N/L-d and 3.0 ± 0.2 mg N/L-d, respec­ tively. The corresponding NO3 −-N utilization rates were 1.3 ± 0.2 mg N/L-d and 1.1 ± 0. mg N/L-d, respectively. Statistical analysis (ANOVA test; p > 0.05) showed that nitrogen-utilization rates were not signifi­ cantly different based on the O2 levels, although NH4 + gave much faster rates than NO3 −. Thus, the methanotrophic biomass was affected more by the N- source than by the DO level. Consistent with the growth results, Fig. 2(b) shows that the methanotrophic biomass consumed all NH4 +-N within 8 days, but ~35% of NO3 −-N remained after 8 days. The stage I results are consistent with several studies that found that methanotrophs supplied with NH4 + grew better than with NO3 −(Chu and Alvarez-Cohen, 1998; Zhang et al., 2017; Bordel et al., 2019b). As NH4 + was the superior N-source, we selected it for the following evaluations of MOM performance.

Fig. 2. Fig. 6 show the microbial community structure at the genus level for stages I (nitrogen sources and DO levels) and II (CH4 pressures for limited DO condition). Methylocystis (up to 87% relative abundance) was the dominant genus initially. Belonging to the family Methylocystaceae, Methylocystis is one of the most common and functionally active CH4- oxidizing bacteria (Webb et al., 2014). Another dominant genus was Hyphomicrobium, which can carry out C1- metabolism and denitrifica­ tion of NO3 −or NO2 −to N2 in anaerobic conditions (Oren and Xu, 2014; Rissanen et al., 2017). Methylocystis and Hyphomicrobium are able to take up NH4 + and NO3 −as nitrogen sources (Nyerges et al., 2010; Brooke et al., 1987). However, they prefer to utilize NH4 + over NO3 −, as their nitrogen-utilization rates showed 2-3-fold difference with NO3 −. Opera­ tion in stage I was nitrogen-replete (NH4 + concentrations, >3 N mg/L), but it became nitrogen deplete (NH4 + concentrations <3 N mg/L) in stage II. At the end of stage II, the relative abundance of Hyphomicrobium increased up to 70% abundance, while Methylocystis become corre­ spondingly less abundant.

captions.caption: FIGURE 1 Construction of the biohybrid MES system based on Rhodopseudomonas palustris for lycopene biosynthesis from CO2 . The engineering strategies consist of intracellular metabolic engineering and extracellular cell-material interfacial engineering to synergistically enhance the supply of electrons and CO2 to R. palustris cells. The carbon flux toward lycopene biosynthesis was enhanced by overexpressing the key genes encoding CrtE, CrtB, and CrtI, highlighted in red. The gene cluster encoding Nif nitrogenase was deleted to block the nitrogen fixation. Tannic acid-modified zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8-TA) was assembled on the R. palustris cell membrane to facilitate CO2 uptake. Dopamine was then polymerized on the R. palustris cell membrane to enhance extracellular electron uptake. Abbreviations: 2-MI, 2-methylimidazole. TA, tannic acid (R denotes the residual moiety of the tannic acid molecule). DA, dopamine. PDA, polydopamine. PioA, cytochrome c-type protein. PioB, decaheme-associated outer membrane protein. PioC, iron sulfur protein. CBB cycle, Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle. G3P, glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. PYR, pyruvate. MEP pathway, methylerythritol phosphate pathway. HMBPP, 1-hydroxy-2-methyl-2-butenyl 4-diphosphate. IPP, isopentenyl diphosphate. DMAPP, dimethylallyl diphosphate. GPP, geranyl diphosphate. FPP, farnesyl diphosphate. GGPP, geranylgeranyl diphosphate. PS I, photosynthetic reaction center. bc1 , cytochrome bc1 complex. UQ, ubiquinone pool. crtI, phytoene desaturase. crtB, phytoene synthase. crtE, geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase.

FIGURE 2 Metabolic engineering strategies for enhanced microbial electrosynthesis of lycopene from CO2 . (a) Schematic of metabolic engineering to redirect intracellular carbon and energy flux toward lycopene biosynthesis. Engineered gene targets are shown in red. Red crosses indicate the corresponding reactions were blocked. Purple arrows represent intracellular energy fluxes. (b) Lycopene production by engineered strains via overexpression of the key genes in the lycopene biosynthesis pathway. The lycopene production was tested after 120 h’ MES operation. (c) Lycopene production and intracellular ATP level in engineered strains after deletion of molybdenum nitrogenase gene cluster. The lycopene production was tested after 120 h’ MES operation. The gene sequence organization of the molybdenum nitrogenase gene cluster and the GenBank accession number were presented. (d) Intracellular level and ratio of reducing equivalents in the engineered strains upon deletion of molybdenum nitrogenase gene cluster. Values and error bars represent the means ± standard deviations of three independent biological replicates. Statistical analysis was conducted using two-tailed Student’s t -test: ** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001.

FIGURE 3 Assembly of ZIF-8-TA on cell membrane of R. palustris to enhance CO2 transfer. (a) Schematic of one-pot assembly of R. palustris -MOF biohybrid. Abbreviations: 2-MI, 2-methylimidazole. TA, tannic acid (R denotes the residual moiety of the tannic acid molecule). (b) SEM images and EDS mappings of biohybrid Z@SRP5 and strain SRP5. The concentration of the Zn2 + ligand was set at 3 mM. Scale bar, 500 nm. (c) XRD analysis of biohybrid Z@SRP5, strain SRP5 and ZIF-8-TA standard. (d) FTIR analysis of biohybrid Z@SRP5, strain SRP5, and ZIF-8-TA standard. (e) CO2 adsorption isotherms of biohybrid Z@SRP5 and strain SRP5. (f) Nyquist curves of biohybrid Z@SRP5 and strain SRP5. (g) Lycopene production by biohybrid Z@SRP5 constructed with different concentrations of ZIF-8-TA ligands. The lycopene production was tested after 120 h’ MES operation. (h) Cell viability of R. palustris treated with different concentrations of Zn2 + ligand, as characterized by live/dead staining. Values and error bars represent the means ± standard deviations of three independent biological replicates. Statistical analysis was conducted using two-tailed Student’s t -test: *** P < 0.001.

FIGURE 4 Polymerization of dopamine on biohybrid Z@SRP5 to enhance EET. (a) Schematic of polymerization of dopamine on the cell membrane of biohybrid Z@SRP5. (b) SEM and TEM images of biohybrids ZP@SRP5 and Z@SRP5. Scale bar, 500 nm. (c) Nyquist curves of biohybrids ZP@SRP5 and Z@SRP5. (d) Cyclic voltammograms of biohybrids ZP@SRP5 and Z@SRP5. Scan rate, 1 mV/s. (e) CLSM images of biofilms formed by biohybrids ZP@SRP5 and Z@SRP5 in MES operation. Scale bar, 10 µm. (f) Lycopene production of biohybrid ZP@SRP5 constructed with different concentrations of dopamine. The lycopene production was tested after 120 h’ MES operation. (g) Intracellular level and ratio of reducing equivalents in biohybrids ZP@SRP5 and Z@SRP5. (h) Proposed mechanism of polydopamine coating for enhancing EET between biohybrid ZP@SRP5 and electrode. The purple matrix represents polydopamine assembled on the cell membrane. (i) Two consecutive MES cycles using biohybrid ZP@SRP5 and strain SRP5. Biomass and lycopene production were assayed every 24 h. (j) Chronoamperometry curves of biohybrid ZP@SRP5 and strain SRP5. The shaded areas around the chronoamperometry curves indicate the error bar range. Values and error bars represent the means ± standard deviations of three independent biological replicates. Statistical analysis was conducted using two-tailed Student’s t -test: * p < 0.05, *** p < 0.001.

FIGURE 5 Molecular mechanism underlying enhanced CO2 fixation and lycopene biosynthesis in biohybrid ZP@SRP5, as revealed by transcriptome analysis. (a) Volcano plot of the transcriptomic data. (b) Differentially expressed genes enriched in energy metabolism and carbon metabolism networks. (c) Transcript abundance changes of genes involved in extracellular electron uptake and conversion in biohybrid ZP@SRP5. Orange and blue rectangles indicate upregulated and downregulated transcripts, respectively. The values represent log2 (Fold Change). (d) Transcript abundance changes of genes involved in the CBB cycle and the lycopene biosynthesis pathway. The transcriptome data were derived from three independent biological replicates.

captions.caption: Figure 1. Electrotrophic lactate production by RAG-1 and enhanced ORR performance in the RAG-1/MR-1 electro-mutualistic system (R&M E- Mut). (a) Organic acid production by RAG-1 and MR-1 under polarized cathodic conditions. (b) 13C-labeled metabolite profiles of RAG-1 cultured under cathodic conditions with NaH13 CO3 as the sole carbon source. (g) EEM fluorescence spectra of culture supernatants. Two protein-like fluorescence regions are highlighted: an additional protein-like fluorescence band at higher excitation wavelengths (T1; Ex ≈270−290 nm, Em ≈320−360 nm) and a canonical tryptophan-like region (T2; Ex = 220−240 nm, Em = 330−360 nm).24

Figure 2. Carbon and energy transfer between species in the RAG-1/MR-1 electro-mutualism. (a) Short-chain fatty acid concentrations in the supernatants of MR-1, RAG-1, and R&M E-Mut cultures. (b) 13C enrichment profiles of intracellular metabolites from the R&M electro- mutualistic system, with NaH13 CO3 provided as the sole carbon source. (c) 13C-labeled metabolites detected in MR-1 grown with lactate as the sole carbon source. (d) Intracellular ATP, total NAD (NADtotal), and NADH/NAD+ ratios quantified from MR-1, RAG-1, and R&M E-Mut. ** indicated p < 0.01 and ns indicated p > 0.05. (e) Under cathodic polarization, RAG-1 fixes inorganic carbon from the bicarbonate−CO2 pool using electrode-derived electrons, generating lactate that serves as a metabolic substrate for MR-1. Heatmaps reflected log2 Fold changes in gene expression related to energy metabolism and EET in each species under electro-mutualism. Numbers 1−5 indicated membrane-associated components of the electron transfer chain: (1) RnfB, (2) complex I, (3) cytochrome bc1 (complex III), (4) terminal oxidase (complex IV), and (5) OmcA.

Figure 3. Riboflavin-enhanced extracellular electron transfer in RAG-1 via interaction with membrane-bound RnfB. (a) Proposed electron transfer pathway in RAG-1 involving riboflavin−RnfB interaction and downstream respiratory complexes. IM, inner membrane; OM, outer membrane. (b) Maximum cathodic current densities of RAG-1 biocathodes supplemented with increasing riboflavin concentrations (0.5−5 μM). (c) Molecular docking model of riboflavin in the quinone-binding pocket of RnfB. (d) NCI analysis of the riboflavin−RnfB complex. (e) Frontier molecular orbital diagrams of free riboflavin and the riboflavin−RnfB complex.

Figure 4. Functional assessment of riboflavin-mediated electron transport in RAG-1 under respiratory inhibition. (a) Schematic diagram of electron transfer pathways in RAG-1 and corresponding inhibition mechanisms. Rotenone (CIi) inhibits NADH oxidation at Complex I; dicoumarol (CoQi) impairs quinone-mediated electron transfer; combined inhibition (CI&CoQi) disrupts riboflavin-driven electron flow by blocking both routes. (b) Maximum cathodic current densities of RAG-1 under each condition with 5 μM riboflavin supplementation. (c) Apparent electron transfer rate constants (Kapp) determined by linear fitting of anodic (Epa) and cathodic (Epc) peak separations under control and inhibitor-treated conditions. (d) CVs of RAG-1 under control and inhibitor-treated conditions, showing characteristic redox features. Annotated peaks correspond to representative anodic and cathodic potentials.

Figure 5. Oxygen reduction performance of the R&M electrode compared to commercial Pt/C and laccase-based electrodes. (a) Electro- mutualistic architecture (role-based schematic). Under cathodic polarization, an electrotroph (“Bio-CPU”) fixes CO2 and produces lactate. The lactate sustains a nonelectrotroph (“electron-accelerator”), which secretes flavins that mediate EET. Flavin−protein interactions (e.g., RnfB) facilitate transmembrane electron entry into the Bio-CPU, routing electrons to the respiratory chain for O2 reduction. Solid purple arrows indicate carbon flow; red dashed arrows indicate electron flow. (b) LSV curves under O2-saturated conditions comparing the R&M cathode with commercial Pt/C and laccase-based electrodes. (c) Comparison of the maximum output current density of the R&M biocathode with that of previously reported oxygen-reducing biocathode catalysts. (d) Tafel plots derived from LSV data, showing different oxygen reduction kinetics among R&M, Pt/C, and laccase electrodes in O2-saturated PBS (pH 7.0). (e) Chronoamperometric stability under constant polarization (−0.2 V vs Ag/AgCl) comparing the durability of the three electrodes.

Ultimately, the model was validated using kinetics data to compare the prediction capabilities of the M-model using growth rates and substrate concentrations for specific time points.
